PullRequest.Title: terminal: cancel pending child process monitor refreshes
PullRequest.Body:
Related to #279177.

### What changed

Make `ChildProcessMonitor` own its pending input debounce and output throttle with registered `RunOnceScheduler`s, so disposal cancels both timers and later input/output cannot reschedule work. Preserve the one-second input quiet period and five-second leading/trailing output timing.

This addresses **bounded retention after disposal**, not a demonstrated permanent Promise cycle. The monitor does not use a reducer, and its debounce result was `undefined` in the measured baseline. Generic decorators, process-tree inspection, error logging, PID updates, and terminal shutdown are unchanged.

### Actual Code OSS verification

Compared fresh isolated Windows Code OSS builds from baseline `373b432de935e02c06d6e930d601b2740bc53987`, using Electron 43.7.3 / Node 24.21.0. Measured real pty-host objects and strong retainer paths, not generic memory totals or callback counts. Each scenario used three warmups, two batches, immediate/post-7.5-second snapshots, and two explicit GCs.

| Scenario, per batch | Baseline immediately after disposal | Candidate | Settled baseline / candidate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 17 completed tasks | 4 disposed monitors | 0 | 0 / 0 |
| 17 actual monitors exercised/disposed inside Code OSS pty host | 17 disposed monitors | 0 | 0 / 0 |
| 17 and 97 interactive terminal create/echo/close cycles | 5 monitor/terminal owners | 5 | 0 / 0 |

The last row is an intentional control: Windows' separate native shutdown grace timer retains the terminal owner temporarily. That path remains unchanged. An already-running process-tree query can also retain its monitor until it completes; this change only cancels pending checks.

Real child-process start/exit/start still reports `[true, false, true]`, with equivalent input debounce, leading output, and trailing output behavior. Historical PID-update, disposal, terminal cleanup, and shared reducer/isolation fixes were inspected and their relevant contracts checked. Original Linux/macOS-specific and forced native-race repros remain unverified.

### Tests and review

- Three focused disposal regressions failed before the fix.
- Four monitor tests and 27 surrounding decorator/event tests pass: **31 passing**.
- `npm run typecheck-client` passes.
- Targeted ESLint passes.
- Two independent read-only full-diff reviews, `gpt-6-astra` and `claude-opus-5.5`, with default effort: no significant findings.
- Full issue/linked-history investigation and all 51 open `freeze-slow-crash-leak` PR file inventories checked; relevant patches/reviews do not provide an adequate pending fix. Refreshed before publication.

Raw heaps, original executed harnesses, screenshots, logs, exact revision/output identities, and the commit/issue-to-scenario evidence matrix are preserved in the originating session's private persistent report. No user profiles or credentials were used.

Scenarios.Scenario: Active terminal input/output updates child-process state
Scenarios.CriticalPath: PTY input/output delivery itself does not await monitoring. After one second of input quiet or the five-second output leading/trailing throttle followed by the one-second debounce, listProcesses must complete before HasChildProcesses can update; this work remains off the terminal data rendering/input critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: On Linux/macOS, resolve and execute ps to enumerate processes; Linux additionally executes cpuUsage.sh for the selected process tree.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Per monitor, repeated input is coalesced to one query after a one-second quiet period. Output causes one leading refresh and at most one trailing refresh per five-second interval. On Linux a successful refresh reaches up to three subprocess executions (which ps, ps/ps.sh, and cpuUsage.sh); macOS reaches two. Effective cardinality is unchanged by the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The decorator-based debounce and throttle invoked the same listProcesses operation with the same one-second debounce and five-second leading/trailing output cadence.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The subprocess sequence delays only the asynchronous child-process-state update, not terminal input/output progress.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: On Windows, dynamically load @vscode/windows-process-tree and query the process list and CPU usage through native callbacks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One native process-tree query sequence per coalesced refresh per terminal; no global limiter across terminals and no change in per-terminal coalescing or aggregate concurrency.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same Windows process-tree and CPU queries ran at the same coalesced refresh cadence before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Completion gates only the child-process-state update and remains asynchronous from terminal I/O.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Input event frequency, output event frequency, number of simultaneously active terminals, and OS process-tree size. Effective calls are reduced by per-monitor debounce/throttle but independent terminals may still query concurrently, exactly as before.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each monitor has one active and one inactive scheduler. Input resets the active scheduler; output maintains one trailing inactive scheduler. Slow listProcesses calls can overlap with later refreshes and different terminals are not globally limited, but neither behavior is introduced or amplified by this change.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No result cache exists. Scheduler state is per monitor; warm module loading may reduce Windows import overhead, but process trees are always re-read. The diff preserves coalescing and does not alter success, empty-result, or failure retry behavior.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: decorator source, RunOnceScheduler source, terminal callers, and listProcesses implementations were traced directly.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact process enumeration time depends on platform and process-tree size, but there is no uncertainty that the diff preserves boundary count and scheduling cadence.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The patch replaces decorator timers with disposable schedulers without increasing process-query frequency, concurrency, or critical-path work.

Scenarios.Scenario: Terminal disposal with pending monitor refreshes
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Disposal synchronously disposes the registered schedulers. No process-tree boundary must complete unless a query had already started before disposal.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of terminals or tasks disposed while input/output timers are pending. Before the diff each pending decorator timer retained its monitor until expiry, with a trailing output callback able to schedule another one-second debounce; after the diff pending timers are canceled immediately.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each disposed monitor can have at most one input and one output timer. Disposal now cancels both; an already-running asynchronous listProcesses call remains uncancelled, as before.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is involved. Cancellation applies to pending scheduler state only and does not fabricate cached child-process results.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: both schedulers are registered in ChildProcessMonitor's DisposableStore, RunOnceScheduler.dispose cancels its timeout and clears its runner, and post-disposal input/output scheduling is guarded.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The amount of reclaimed object-graph memory and frequency of rapid terminal churn vary by workload; retention duration and timer ownership are directly established.
Scenarios.Verdict: This is a performance improvement, not a regression: pending timer roots and delayed callbacks are removed on disposal while in-flight process queries remain unchanged.

Analysis.Summary: Reviewed the full two-file diff under the performance focus. Traced input, output, disposal, scheduler/decorator semantics, terminal ownership, and platform-specific process-tree boundaries. No actionable performance regression was introduced; the change preserves coalescing and expensive-boundary cardinality while reducing bounded post-disposal retention.
